title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 81
paragraphs: So in sending to his other allies, he sent also to Lacedaemon. But these—the Spartans, I mean—had at this very time (as it happened) a quarrel of their own in hand with the Argives about the district called Thyrea. For the Lacedaemonians had cut off this Thyrea, which was part of the Argive territory, and had taken it for themselves. At that time the Argives possessed the whole region toward the west extending as far down as Malea, both the parts on the mainland and also the island of Cythera with the other islands. When the Argives had come to the rescue to save their territory from being cut off, the two sides came to a parley and agreed that three hundred men should fight on each side, and whichever side had the better in the fight, that nation should possess the disputed land. They also agreed that the main body of each army should withdraw to its own country and not stand by while the contest was fought, for fear that, if the armies were present, one side, seeing their countrymen suffering defeat, would come up to their support. Having made this agreement, they withdrew, and chosen men of both sides were left behind and engaged in combat with one another. They fought and proved themselves evenly matched, and at last, of six hundred men, only three were left alive—on the Argive side Alcenor and Chromius, and on the Lacedaemonian side Othryades. These were left alive when night came on. The two Argives, supposing that they were the victors, set off to run back to Argos; but the Lacedaemonian Othryades, after stripping the corpses of the Argives and carrying their arms to his own camp, remained in his place. On the next day both sides came to the spot to inquire about the result, and for some time both claimed the victory for themselves: the one side saying that more of them had survived, the others declaring that those men had fled whereas their own man had stood his ground and had stripped the corpses of the other party. At length, because of this dispute, they fell upon one another and began to fight again, and after many had fallen on both sides, the Lacedaemonians were victorious. The Argives then cut their hair short, whereas formerly they were required by law to wear it long, and they made a law with a curse attached: that from that time forth no Argive man should grow his hair long nor their women wear ornaments of gold until they had won back Thyrea. The Lacedaemonians, on the contrary, laid down for themselves the opposite law: that they should wear long hair from that time forward, whereas before that time they had not worn it long. And they say that the one man left alive of the three hundred, Othryades, being ashamed to return to Sparta when all his comrades had been slain, killed himself there in Thyrea.
